title: Ayodhya And After
byline: by Koenraad Elst · Voice of India · 1991 · subtitled Issues Before Hindu Society
lede: Elst's second book on Ayodhya was written during the 1990–91 crisis. He starts from the temple question, which he considers settled, and moves to what Ayodhya revealed: how the press reported it, the riots, the meaning of secularism, book bans, the charge of “Hindu fascism”, and what the Hindu movement should stand for. He writes as a Belgian who is, in his words, neither Hindu nor Muslim.
facts: chapters plus two appendices, built largely on press coverage from 1989–91
the mosque's date; Elst suggests Mir Baqi may have found ruins left by Ghori's army of 1194
the Kar Seva, when kar sevaks got through Mulayam Singh Yadav's blockade
appendices, giving the last word to Girilal Jain and Ram Swarup
note: Elst writes as an open sympathiser of the Ram Janmabhoomi movement. Some chapters, notably the one on riots, make sweeping claims about a whole community. This page reports them as his claims, does not repeat his harshest language, and does not endorse it.

items: Elst allows that they may already have destroyed the temple.
On Babur's orders, per the Persian inscriptions. Elst rejects the JNU historians' doubts about who built it.
Two of the four pre-1800 sources Elst cites: European travellers who record Hindu worship and the demolition tradition.
Found in 1990–91, along with an early-18th-century text by Aurangzeb's granddaughter.
The Hindu side says it was not used as a mosque after 1936. Hindus took it over in 1949.
Worship of Ram Lalla becomes public.
Foundation stone laid. In Bangladesh, more than 200 temples are destroyed in reaction, Elst reports.
Elst notes the procession itself saw no riots, unlike much of Uttar Pradesh.
Kar sevaks reach the site despite arrests, curfews and suspended transport. Many are shot.
The Chandra Shekhar government asks both sides for evidence. VHP-invited scholars find more documents.
Written while the Ayodhya issue “became a symbol”.

sections.eyebrow: Chapter 1 · summary of the historical question
sections.title: Elst's chain of evidence
sections.lede: He treats each kind of evidence as a separate link, so the case does not rest on any single one.
items: B.B. Lal and S.P. Gupta: 11th-century pillar bases aligned with the mosque.
Persian inscriptions name Babur and Mir Baqi.
Western travellers and local Muslim writers record the tradition.
Hindus kept worshipping in the courtyard under Muslim rule.
Elst finds no sign the British invented it after 1800 to justify annexing Awadh.

sections.eyebrow: Chapters 2–4 · belief, history and the law
sections.title: Should the wrongs of history be righted?
sections.lede: Elst separates the historical question (was there a temple?) from the questions of belief and law.

items: Proof of a Ram temple is not proof that Ram was born on that exact spot.
Hindus should not try to reclaim all of the thousands of temple sites.
A law freezing places of worship as of 15 August 1947 is a possible part of a deal.
Three sites are special: Ayodhya, Kashi and Mathura.
A gesture from Muslims has to start from admitting the wrong.
Elsewhere in the world, native peoples win back sacred sites in court.
Courts set up under the 1950 Constitution may not be the right place to settle a civilisational dispute.

sections.title: Charges against the Hindu movement, and Elst's replies
head: The charge
Elst's reply
rows: The temple story is a British invention
Four of the sources predate 1800, and Gyanendra Pandey's own study of nearby Varanasi shows no British rumour-mongering.
Calling the Ram temple a Buddhist stupa (Savita Ambedkar) cannot fit a pillared building.
Mahmud is revered by Muslims as a devout warrior of the faith.
No evidence links Advani to Hitler. The swastika is pan-Asian and pre-Hindu as well as Hindu.
Neither the court nor the prosecutor implicated the RSS.
The RSS collaborated with the British in 1942
The Communists were the ones who backed the British, after Hitler invaded the USSR.
Bans on Rushdie and on Ram Swarup's book on the Hadis show secularism protecting one creed from criticism.

sections.title: What secularism should mean, in Elst's view
items: There it meant freeing thought and society from Church dogma, not equal respect for all creeds.
A recent coinage of Gandhi's, Elst says, not traditional Hindu doctrine.
The official Hindi word means neutrality towards dharma itself. Elst prefers “sect-neutrality”.
He argues the separation of spiritual and temporal power is an old Indian idea, not an 18th-century European one.

sections.title: From Ayodhya to Indraprastha
sections.lede: Elst calls Ayodhya a symbol and urges the movement to go beyond it, with a programme of its own.
items: Answer the charge of theocracy with stated values and goals.
“Justice for all, appeasement of none”: a human rights commission instead of a minorities commission.
Be proud of Hinduism rather than calling it “integral humanism” to sound secular.
Change the intellectual climate, and leave it to the parties to follow.

sections.q: This is a thousand-year-old civilizational problem which has not been resolved.
